lxc_b53508d696554ff3.text: Follow Lithuania from its earliest written name through major changes in statehood to its landscape, language, and culture today.

lxc_fa5f955413a192b7.text: The earliest known written record of Lithuania’s name comes from the Annals of Quedlinburg.

lxc_13394c5016f456c8.text: It described events from 9 March 1009 and used the Latin form *Litua*.

lxc_6db826ddcb8591cf.text: However, this record was not the beginning of the Lithuanian people.

lxc_d8e03922e75db2f0.text: It was simply the first surviving written mention.

lxc_b702c7a1a7122aa4.text: The exact meaning of *Lietuva* is still debated.

lxc_49c4c633343c9b6e.text: One theory connects it to the small Lietava River near Kernavė.

lxc_1e47a14a6c6fb4b0.text: Another connects it to the *leičiai*, a historical warrior group.

lxc_fa848ecad8f220a8.text: Lithuanian is an East Baltic language related to Latvian, although speakers of the two languages cannot automatically understand each other.

lxc_8e653dc0e8046642.text: It preserves some very old features of the Indo-European language family.

lxc_44d13bfcbcfcabb5.text: In the 13th century, Baltic tribes in Aukštaitija formed a pagan state.

lxc_48631199e5aa7af6.text: Mindaugas was crowned the Catholic King of Lithuania on 6 July 1253, although he later returned to pagan practice.

lxc_aa792818ffac576c.text: The Grand Duchy of Lithuania developed from this early state.

lxc_4fd1a96842165bc3.text: Gediminas made Vilnius the lasting capital from 1323.

lxc_479791508bde8039.text: During the 14th and 15th centuries, the Grand Duchy became one of Europe’s largest states.

lxc_f1b80240a405330c.text: Around 1430, it stretched from the Baltic Sea toward the Black Sea and covered about 930,000 square kilometres.

lxc_a64656bdfdcbd413.text: Lithuania was the last major pagan state in Europe.

lxc_af39dd14a4201c06.text: After Jogaila signed the Union of Krewo in 1385, Lithuania was Christianized in 1387.

lxc_5a881255d4bce45c.text: In 1410, Polish–Lithuanian forces defeated the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald.

lxc_2a4313fb559026d9.text: The Union of Lublin created the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1569.

lxc_a5e723985ea56f0c.text: Lithuania shared a state with Poland but kept its own laws, army, and treasury.

lxc_76a94f3f2216c90f.text: After three partitions, the Third Partition ended the state in 1795, and the Russian Empire took most Lithuanian lands, including Vilnius.

lxc_37ebe8c16f5df247.text: Russia banned Lithuanian books printed in the Latin alphabet from 1864.

lxc_e8363dbc4342cc24.text: Book smugglers, called *knygnešiai*, secretly carried such books from East Prussia.

lxc_71676f973f60b6da.text: On 16 February 1918, twenty members of the Council of Lithuania signed the Act of Independence in Vilnius.

lxc_3671ba0d93a105db.text: The Act restored an independent democratic Lithuanian state with Vilnius as its capital.

lxc_f849ded143ef1b4a.text: In August 1939, the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact placed the Baltic states in the Soviet sphere.

lxc_15a5f64fe3c1f18a.text: The Soviet Union occupied Lithuania in June 1940.

lxc_2c18d8f867f84371.text: Nazi Germany occupied it in 1941, and Soviet forces returned in 1944.

lxc_8cdb000d46b62722.text: Anti-Soviet partisans continued fighting into the early 1950s, while about 130,000 Lithuanians were deported to Siberia.

lxc_f6b2367184bfcac7.text: On 11 March 1990, Lithuania declared the restoration of independence.

lxc_e767c1632773fac3.text: “Restoration” was important: the Act stated that the independence declared in 1918 had never legally lost its force.

lxc_283f8c6a8c560297.text: Moscow responded with an economic blockade.

lxc_1dd19185ba99b13b.text: On 13 January 1991, Soviet forces attacked important buildings in Vilnius, killing fourteen unarmed people.

lxc_7b843fec4dfa4f79.text: The Soviet Union recognized Lithuania on 6 September 1991, and the last Russian army units left in 1993.

lxc_63f8305344a62d11.text: Modern Lithuania is a country of about 2.9 million people on the eastern Baltic Sea.

lxc_27b7d259b701f35e.text: Its capital is Vilnius, Lithuanian is its official language, and Klaipėda is its main port.

lxc_6cf59b9bb43e2607.text: Forests cover about one third of the land, and there are more than 3,000 lakes.

lxc_69a0f5743678a5dc.text: Lithuania joined NATO and the European Union in 2004.

lxc_afd63be76a34eb77.text: It entered the eurozone in 2015, so it uses the euro.

lxc_b6e075e50d52b4f3.text: These memberships connect the restored state closely with European and transatlantic institutions.

lxc_743674601c379ffb.text: Older history remains visible in modern culture.

lxc_fc7e3de8ad5bf13c.text: Baltic amber was once traded to the Roman Empire, and Palanga now has an amber museum.

lxc_a82099403876eaa0.text: The Hill of Crosses near Šiauliai became a symbol of Catholic resistance during the Soviet period.
